description: "A visual story examining what Pacific places manage despite accounting for 0.0454% of territorial carbon dioxide emissions"
---

```{=html}
<header class="hero">
  <div class="hero-water" aria-hidden="true"></div>
  <div class="hero-inner">
    <p class="eyebrow">A Pacific climate data story</p>
    <h1>Living with a Changing Climate Across the Pacific</h1>
    <p class="hero-lede">How can a region responsible for such a small share of emissions have so much to manage?</p>
    <div class="hero-pair" aria-label="Pacific and world territorial carbon dioxide emissions in 2023 from Our World in Data">
      <article>
        <span class="hero-place">17 covered Pacific places</span>
        <strong>17.3 million t</strong>
        <span>territorial CO₂ in 2023</span>
      </article>
      <article>
        <span class="hero-place">World</span>
        <strong>38.1 billion t</strong>
        <span>territorial CO₂ in 2023</span>
      </article>
    </div>
    <p class="hero-share"><strong>0.0454%</strong><span>of the world total came from the 17 Pacific island countries and territories covered by the dataset.</span></p>
  </div>
</header>

<nav class="chapter-nav" aria-label="Story chapters">
  <a href="#emissions">Contribution</a>
  <a href="#impact">Consequences</a>
  <a href="#cyclones">Cyclones</a>
  <a href="#warming">Warming</a>
  <a href="#reefs">Coral heat</a>
  <a href="#sea">Sea level</a>
  <a href="#rain">Rain and crops</a>
  <a href="#response">Response</a>
</nav>

<main>
  <section id="emissions" class="chapter chapter-light">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">01</p>
      <h2>Pacific territorial CO₂ in the 2023 world total</h2>
      <p>The first bar preserves the world scale. The second enlarges its first 0.1% so the covered Pacific share can be seen.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="emissions-chart" class="viz-frame" role="img" aria-label="True-scale and magnified comparisons of Pacific and world territorial carbon dioxide emissions in 2023"></div>
    <aside class="reading-note">
      <strong>A like-for-like comparison</strong>
      <p>Both figures count territorial CO₂ in 2023 using the same Our World in Data release. They do not cover consumption-based emissions, emissions from land-use change or greenhouse gases other than CO₂. Five Pacific places in the project list had no 2023 value and are not included in the regional total.</p>
    </aside>
  </section>

  <section id="impact" class="chapter chapter-impact">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">02</p>
      <h2>Reported human and economic effects of four cyclones</h2>
      <p>Event assessments report 65,000 people displaced by Cyclone Pam, 540,400 affected by Winston, about 80,000 affected by Gita and about 130,000 affected by Harold. Each assessment put the reported economic effects or losses above one-fifth of annual GDP; Pam’s assessment reached 64.1%.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="event-cards" class="event-grid" aria-label="Human and economic consequences reported for four Pacific cyclones"></div>
    <aside class="reading-note impact-note">
      <strong>Different reports use different measures</strong>
      <p>Affected people, displacement, damage and wider economic effects are not the same measure. The figures describe individual events and should not be added together or treated as a time series.</p>
    </aside>
  </section>

  <section id="cyclones" class="chapter chapter-map">
    <div class="chapter-copy chapter-copy-map">
      <p class="chapter-number">03</p>
      <h2>South Pacific cyclone tracks from 1980 to 2023</h2>
      <p>IBTrACS records 508 storm tracks across the South Pacific from 1980 to 2023. Of these, 103 reached Category 3 or above in the archive’s USA intensity field. The map places the four event assessments within the wider regional record, but it does not test whether cyclone frequency or intensity changed over time.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="cyclone-scrolly" class="scrolly">
      <div class="scrolly-sticky">
        <svg id="cyclone-map" viewBox="0 0 1000 600" role="img" aria-label="South Pacific tropical cyclone tracks from 1980 through 2023"></svg>
        <div id="cyclone-legend" class="map-legend"></div>
      </div>
      <div class="scrolly-steps">
        <article class="step" data-view="all">
          <p class="step-label">All tracks</p>
          <h3>The archive contains 508 South Pacific storm tracks</h3>
          <p>The archive begins well before the period shown here. The 1980 start keeps the view inside the modern satellite era.</p>
        </article>
        <article class="step" data-view="intensity">
          <p class="step-label">Recorded intensity</p>
          <h3>The archive classifies 103 tracks as Category 3 or above</h3>
          <p>The categories use the IBTrACS USA Saffir Simpson field. Agency wind standards differ, so this is an orientation layer rather than a trend test.</p>
        </article>
        <article class="step" data-view="events">
          <p class="step-label">Event assessments</p>
          <h3>The highlighted tracks are Pam, Winston, Gita and Harold</h3>
          <p>These are the four tracks linked to the event reports shown immediately before the map.</p>
        </article>
      </div>
    </div>
  </section>

  <section id="warming" class="chapter chapter-dark">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">04</p>
      <h2>Sea-surface temperatures were higher in the recent decade</h2>
      <p>Across all 21 places with complete data, the sea surface was warmer on average from 2014 to 2023 than from 1993 to 2002. The increase ranged from 0.21°C in French Polynesia to 0.49°C in Nauru. The rows below keep each place separate rather than replacing them with a single Pacific average.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="sst-chart" class="viz-frame viz-frame-dark" role="img" aria-label="Comparison of early and recent sea-surface temperature anomalies for 21 Pacific places"></div>
    <aside class="reading-note reading-note-dark">
      <strong>A change in average conditions</strong>
      <p>The comparison shows the direction and size of the temperature shift. It does not measure how the change affected particular communities or ecosystems.</p>
    </aside>
  </section>

  <section id="reefs" class="chapter chapter-dark">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">05</p>
      <h2>Annual coral heat stress at eight Pacific virtual stations</h2>
      <p>Degree Heating Weeks combine how far temperatures rise above the local bleaching threshold with how long the heat persists. Annual maximum values reached or exceeded 4°C-weeks in multiple years and locations, while the timing and size of the peaks differed among stations.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="reef-chart" class="viz-frame viz-frame-dark" role="img" aria-label="Annual maximum Degree Heating Weeks at eight Pacific reef virtual stations from 1985 through 2025"></div>
    <aside class="reading-note reading-note-dark">
      <strong>An accumulated heat-stress measure</strong>
      <p>At 4°C-weeks, significant coral bleaching can occur; at 8°C-weeks, severe bleaching and coral mortality become likely. Degree Heating Weeks indicate heat stress, while observations at the reef are still needed to confirm whether bleaching occurred.</p>
    </aside>
  </section>

  <section id="sea" class="chapter chapter-dark">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">06</p>
      <h2>The sea level record moves into higher bands</h2>
      <p>In 2023, all 21 records reported a positive anomaly: 20 were reported at +0.1 metre and Vanuatu at +0.2 metre. Higher bands became more common across the 1993-2023 period, although the source values are rounded to the nearest 0.1 metre.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="sea-chart" class="viz-frame viz-frame-dark" role="img" aria-label="Sea-level anomaly bands for 21 Pacific places from 1993 through 2023"></div>
    <aside class="reading-note reading-note-dark">
      <strong>A broad regional measure</strong>
      <p>The rounding makes transitions look abrupt and hides smaller changes. Local shorelines also respond to waves, storms, sediment and vertical land movement, so these records should not be read as local flood levels.</p>
    </aside>
  </section>

  <section id="rain" class="chapter chapter-light">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">07</p>
      <h2>Annual rainfall and crop-yield changes across 15 Pacific places</h2>
      <p>Across 450 paired country-years, the Pearson correlation between annual rainfall anomalies and year-to-year changes in reported crop yield was 0.04. Wetter years included both yield gains and losses, and the same was true in drier years.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="rain-chart" class="viz-frame" role="img" aria-label="Annual rainfall anomalies and crop-yield changes across 450 paired country-years in 15 Pacific places"></div>
    <aside class="reading-note">
      <strong>What the weak correlation means</strong>
      <p>National annual values remove the timing and location of rainfall, while crop yields also vary with conditions that are not represented on this chart. The result does not show that rainfall is unimportant; it shows that one national rainfall anomaly is not enough to explain annual yield changes.</p>
    </aside>
  </section>

  <section id="response" class="chapter chapter-light chapter-response">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">08</p>
      <h2>Renewable electricity generation across 18 Pacific places in 2023</h2>
      <p>In 2023, renewables supplied 94.4% of recorded electricity in Tokelau and 52.1% in Fiji. They were the only two of 18 places where renewables passed the halfway mark. The chart covers electricity generation rather than transport fuels and other energy uses, which are tracked separately</p>
    </div>
    <div id="energy-chart" class="viz-frame" role="img" aria-label="Renewable share of electricity generation in 18 Pacific places in 2023"></div>
    <aside class="reading-note response-note">
      <strong>Reading the 2023 response</strong>
      <p>The chart does not show how quickly each electricity system is changing. It shows the renewable share recorded in 2023 and the different starting points for further change.</p>
    </aside>
  </section>
```
